records.themeSummary: Recognizing divine help includes recognizing the source of one’s own spiritual effort.
records.originHebrew: וְאַחַר כָּל אֵלֶּה נִצְרָךְ עוֹד תְּפִלָּה לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיַּעֲזוֹר לוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּגְּמָרָא (שָׁם): וְאִלְמָלֵא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שֶׁעוֹזֵר לוֹ, אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לוֹ. אַךְ תְּפִלָּה וְיִרְאָה הֵם דָּבָר אֶחָד. דְּיִרְאָה בָּא עַל יְדֵי שֶׁמְּצַיֵּיר הָאָדָם לְפָנָיו שֶׁמֶּלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹמֵד עָלָיו וְרוֹאֶה בְּמַעֲשָׂיו, וְאָז מִיָּד יַגִּיעַ אֵלָיו הַיִּרְאָה (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב רֵישׁ אֹרַח חַיִּים). וּכְשֶׁעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ מְבַקֵּשׁ רַחֲמִים עַל צְרָכָיו.
records.originEnglish: After all these things, one still needs prayer to Hashem, blessed be He, that He help him, as they said in the Gemara there: “Were the Holy One, blessed be He, not helping him, he could not overcome it.” Prayer and awe are one thing: awe comes through a person picturing the supreme King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, standing over him and seeing his deeds. Awe then immediately reaches him, as stated at the beginning of Orach Chayim. And when he stands before the King, he seeks mercy for his needs.
records.targetRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 3:1
records.targetHebrew: עֵת מְצוֹא, מוֹרֶה עַל דָּבָר תַּכְלִיתִי, שֶׁתַּכְלִית כָּל עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא עוֹלָם הַסָּפֵק וּמָלֵא הֶסְתֵּר הוּא, שֶׁיְּבָרֵר הָאָדָם אֶת עַצְמוֹ כְּפִי כֹּחוֹ, וְאַחַר כָּל זֶה יִצְרַךְ לְהַתְּפִלָּה, לְהִתְפַּלֵּל לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיִּגְמוֹר בַּעֲדוֹ לְטוֹב. כִּי כָּל בֵּירוּרֵי הָאָדָם שֶׁמְּבָרֵר אֶת עַצְמוֹ כְּפִי כֹּחוֹ וְהַשָּׂגַת שִׂכְלוֹ, כּוּלָּם כְּאַיִן נֶחְשָׁבוּ, מֵאַחַר שֶׁכָּל עִיקַּר הַבְּרִיאָה בְּרֵאשִׁיתָהּ נִבְרֵאת יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן, לָזֶה צָרִיךְ לִתְפִלָּה לְהִתְפַּלֵּל לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אַחַר כָּל הַבֵּירוּרִין, וְיִמְסוֹר נַפְשׁוֹ וּמְאוֹדוֹ לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, לְהַכִּיר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא הַנּוֹתֵן בּוֹ כֹּחַ לַעֲשׂוֹת חָיִל אַף בַּעֲבוֹדוֹת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וּבֵירוּרָיו.
records.targetEnglish: “A time of finding” points to an ultimate purpose: the purpose of all the affairs of this world, a world of uncertainty full of concealment, is that a person refine himself as far as his strength permits. After all this, he will need prayer, praying to Hashem, blessed be He, to bring matters to a good conclusion for him. For all the refinements a person achieves according to his strength and intellectual grasp count as nothing, since creation itself was originally brought into being from nothing. He therefore needs to pray to Hashem after all his refinements, surrendering his soul and all his resources to Him and recognizing that Hashem gives him the strength to accomplish—even in his service of Hashem and his own refinements.
records.explanation: Pri Tzadik places prayer after Torah and the disciplined struggle with desire. Beit Yaakov explains why effort cannot make prayer unnecessary: the person’s very capacity to refine himself is a divine gift. The full section continues to insist on preparation and refinement, so this comparison does not replace effort with passivity.

records.themeTitle: Desire as the power of spiritual growth
records.themeSummary: The power that can become craving also makes sustained growth in Torah possible.
records.originHebrew: וְעִיקַּר הַהַגְדָּרָה מִפְּגַם הַתַּאֲוָה הוּא עַל יְדֵי תוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (קִידּוּשִׁין ל:): בָּרָאתִי יֵצֶר הָרָע וּבָרָאתִי לוֹ תּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין וְכוּלֵי, אִם פָּגַע בְּךָ מְנֻוָּול זֶה, מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ. שֶׁעִיקַּר בְּרִיאַת הַיֵּצֶר, שֶׁהוּא הַחֵשֶׁק, הָיָה כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה חֲמִידוּ דְאוֹרַיְיתָא, לִהְיוֹת חֶדְוָותָא דִשְׁמַעְתָּא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לֶעָתִיד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (זֹהַר חֵלֶק א קלח א בְּמִדְרַשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם).
records.originEnglish: The principal protection against the damage of desire is through Torah, as they said in Kiddushin 30b: “I created the evil inclination, and I created Torah as its seasoning,” and so forth; “If this repulsive one encounters you, draw him to the study hall.” For the inclination, which is the power of longing, was chiefly created to become longing for Torah and the joy of learning, as it will be in the future, as stated in the Zohar, volume I, 138a, in Midrash HaNe’elam.
records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Bereshit 15
records.targetHebrew: וּכְמוֹ כֵן בְּנֶפֶשׁ הַטִּיפָּה הָרִאשׁוֹנָה שֶׁל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁנִּכְנֶסֶת בָּאָדָם יִקָּרֵא צֶלֶם, וְהַתְּשׁוּקָה שֶׁמִּשְׁתּוֹקֵק לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה יִקָּרֵא דְּמוּת וְעַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּקָה נִתּוֹסֵף לוֹ בְּכָל פַּעַם יוֹתֵר דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְזֶה "בְּיוֹם בְּרוֹא אֱלֹקִים אָדָם בִּדְמוּת אֱלֹקִים" וְכוּלֵי, הַיְינוּ כִּי זֶה הָיָה עִקָּר בְּרִיאַת הָאָדָם בִּכְדֵי שֶׁיִּשְׁתּוֹקֵק בְּכָל פַּעַם לְהִתְרַבּוּת דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְזֶה עִנְיַן (בְּרָכוֹת ז:) גָּדוֹל שִׁמּוּשָׁהּ שֶׁל תּוֹרָה יוֹתֵר מִלִּמּוּדָהּ, שִׁמּוּשָׁהּ שֶׁל תּוֹרָה נִקְרֵאת הַתְּשׁוּקָה.
records.targetEnglish: Likewise in the soul, the first drop of words of Torah that enters a person is called “image,” while the longing with which he longs for words of Torah is called “likeness.” Through that longing, more words of Torah are continually added to him. This is “On the day God created man, in the likeness of God,” and so forth: the essential purpose of creating the person was that he should constantly long for an increase in words of Torah. This is the meaning of “Serving Torah is greater than studying it” in Berakhot 7b: serving Torah is the name given to longing.
records.explanation: Pri Tzadik identifies the original purpose of desire as delight in Torah. Mei HaShiloach supplies a developmental account: an initial gift of Torah becomes living growth through renewed longing, just as a child’s appetite supports bodily growth. Its interpretation of “serving Torah” is the author’s own homiletic reading.

records.themeSummary: Prayer against being cut off and brokenhearted closeness are related but distinct movements.
records.originHebrew: וְכֵן הַתִּיקּוּן עַל יְדֵי צְעָקָה וּתְפִלָּה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: פְּנֵי הַשֵּׁם בְּעוֹשֵׂי רָע, שֶׁמְּרַמֵּז עַל פְּגָם זֶה שֶׁנִּקְרָא רָע כַּיָּדוּעַ. וּכְתִיב: צָעֲקוּ וְהַשֵּׁם שָׁמֵעַ, דִּצְעָקָה מוֹעִיל. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ב כ א): גְּדוֹלָה צְעָקָה מִכּוּלָּן, שֶׁצְּעָקָה הִיא בַּלֵּב, הֲדָא הוּא דִכְתִיב: צָעַק לִבָּם וְגוֹמֵר, וְעַיֵּן שָׁם דְּמַסִּיק: וּלְעוֹלָם לֹא הַדְרָא רֵיקַנְיָא. וְהַיְינוּ דְּמוֹעִיל אַף לִפְגָם זֶה, שֶׁמָּנַע הַתְּשׁוּבָה מִמֶּנּוּ בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק א ריט ב).
records.originEnglish: Repair also comes through crying out and prayer, as it says, “Hashem’s face is against those who do evil,” alluding to this blemish, which is called evil, as is known. And it is written, “They cried out, and Hashem heard”: crying out is effective. As the holy Zohar, volume II, 20a, states: “Crying out is greater than them all, for crying out is in the heart,” as it is written, “Their heart cried out,” and so forth. See there, where it concludes that it never returns empty. It therefore helps even for this blemish, from which repentance was withheld in the holy Zohar, volume I, 219b.
records.targetHebrew: לֵב נִשְׁבָּר – לִהְיוֹת מַמָּשׁ כְּאַיִן, שֶׁהוּא בַּכֶּתֶר כַּנּוֹדָע שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה עוֹד, וְזֶה מוֹעִיל, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "פְּנֵי ה' בְּעֹשֵׂי רָע", הוּא עָוֹן זֶה שֶׁנִּקְרָא כֵּן, "לְהַכְרִית מֵאֶרֶץ וְגוֹמֵר", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְעַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים לְעוֹלָם יִירְשׁוּ אָרֶץ]", שֶׁיְּרֻשַּׁת הָאָרֶץ הוּא רַק לַצַּדִּיק דְּהַיְינוּ שׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית. וְאָמַר: "צָעֲקוּ וְגוֹמֵר" – תְּפִלָּה הוּא עֵצָה נֶגֶד לְהַכְרִית מֵאֶרֶץ [שֶׁהַתְּפִלָּה שָׁרְשָׁהּ בַּמַּלְכוּת שֶׁהִיא אֶרֶץ הָעֶלְיוֹנָה, וּפְגָמוֹ הִגִּיעַ לָהּ כְּעִנְיַן "ה' צִלְּךָ", מַמָּשׁ דּוּגְמַת הַצֵּל עוֹשֶׂה מַה שֶּׁהוּא עוֹשֶׂה אִם לְטוֹב אִם לְהֵיפֶךְ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם]; אֲבָל לִהְיוֹת קָרוֹב לַה', הָעֵצָה – שְׁבִירוּת לֵב: "וְאֶת דַּכְּאֵי רוּחַ וְגוֹמֵר".
records.targetEnglish: A broken heart—to become truly as nothing, which, as is known, belongs to Keter, higher still—is effective. As it is written, “Hashem’s face is against those who do evil”: this is the sin so called; “to cut off from the land,” and so forth, as it is written, “Your people are all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever”—for inheritance of the land belongs only to the righteous person, meaning one who guards the covenant. And it says, “They cried out,” and so forth: prayer is a remedy against being cut off from the land. Prayer is rooted in Malchut, the supernal land, and his damage has reached it, in the manner of “Hashem is your shadow”: precisely as a shadow does what he does, whether for good or, Heaven forbid, the reverse. But to be close to Hashem, the counsel is brokenheartedness: “And with the contrite of spirit,” and so forth.
records.explanation: Both passages confront the Zohar’s apparent exclusion of repentance for damage to the covenant. Tzidkat HaTzadik distinguishes the protection afforded by prayer from the renewed closeness associated with a broken heart, and places Torah, repentance, and contrition at different spiritual levels. This adds precision to Pri Tzadik’s assurance that the heart’s cry remains effective.

records.themeTitle: One desire, two ways of seeing the world
records.themeSummary: The heart’s apparent division is connected to whether creation is seen as separate from its Creator.
records.originHebrew: וּכְבָר נִתְבָּאֵר שֶׁיֵּצֶר פֵּירוּשׁוֹ חֵשֶׁק, כְּמוֹ לְיֵצֶר מַחְשְׁבוֹת לְבַב עַמֶּךָ. וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בָּרָא הַחֵשֶׁק לִהְיוֹת חֲמִידוּ דְאוֹרַיְיתָא, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לֶעָתִיד (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק א קלח עַמּוּד א), רַק אַתָּה עוֹשֶׂה אוֹתוֹ רָע. וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (קִידּוּשִׁין ל עַמּוּד ב): בָּרָאתִי יֵצֶר הָרָע וּבָרָאתִי לוֹ תּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין. וְאָמְרוּ: אִם פָּגַע בְּךָ מְנֻוָּול זֶה, מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ. וְהַיְינוּ לִהְיוֹת הַחֵשֶׁק וְהַיֵּצֶר לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ, לִהְיוֹת חֶדְוָותָא דִשְׁמַעְתָּא. וְאִם כֵּן נִבְרָא רַק יֵצֶר אֶחָד, וְאֵיךְ קָאָמַר שֶׁבָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שְׁנֵי יְצָרִים? אַכָל הַמְכֻוָּון בָּזֶה עַל שְׁנֵי חַלְלֵי הַלֵּב, וּכְתִיב: לֵב חָכָם לִימִינוֹ וְלֵב כְּסִיל לִשְׂמֹאלוֹ.
records.originEnglish: It has already been explained that yetzer means longing, as in “the inclination of the thoughts of Your people’s heart.” The Holy One, blessed be He, created longing to be longing for Torah, as it will be in the future, as stated in Zohar I, 138a; only you make it evil. Of this they said in Kiddushin 30b: “I created the evil inclination and created Torah as its seasoning.” They also said: “If this repulsive one encounters you, draw him to the study hall”—that the longing and inclination should be directed to the study hall, becoming the joy of learning. If so, only one inclination was created; how can he say that the Holy One created two inclinations? The intention concerns the heart’s two chambers, as it is written: “The wise person’s heart is to his right, and the fool’s heart to his left.”
records.targetRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 9:1
records.targetHebrew: וְלָכֵן בֵּי״ת דִּ"בְּרֵאשִׁית" רַבָּתִי [בְּרֵאשִׁית א׳:א׳], כִּי בְּרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם בְּבֵי״ת, הַיְינוּ דְּאָלֶ״ף הוּא יִחוּדוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה יָחִיד וּמְיֻחָד עַד שֶׁלֹּא נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם; וְהַבְּרִיאָה הָיְתָה לִהְיוֹת נִרְאֶה כְּאִלּוּ יֵשׁ שְׁנַיִם: בּוֹרֵא וְנִבְרָא; רַק בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל יְקַבְּלוּ הַתּוֹרָה הַמַּתְחֶלֶת בְּאָלֶ״ף דְּ"אָנֹכִי וְגוֹמֵר" [שְׁמוֹת כ׳:ב׳], לְהַכִּיר שֶׁגַּם עַתָּה, מִשֶּׁנִּבְרָא הָעוֹלָם, ה' אֶחָד כְּעַד שֶׁלֹּא נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם. וְזֶהוּ מִצַּד הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁהוּא קִיּוּם הָעוֹלָם, אֲבָל מִצַּד הָעוֹלָם הוּא הַבֵּי״ת. וְהַתְחָלַת הַכָּרַת הַבֵּי״ת הוּא בַּלֵּב, דְּשָׁם שְׁנֵי חֲלָלִים לְמִשְׁכַּן שְׁנֵי יְצָרִים: וְהַיֵּצֶר הָרָע מַרְאֶה שֶׁהֵם שְׁנַיִם, וּמַפְרִיד חַס וְשָׁלוֹם הַבְּרִיאָה מִן הַבּוֹרֵא; וְהַיֵּצֶר טוֹב מַדְרִיכוֹ לָדַעַת כִּי בֶאֱמֶת ה' אֶחָד וְאֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ.
records.targetEnglish: The bet of “Bereshit” is therefore enlarged, for the world was created with bet. Alef is the unity of the world, as He was alone and unique before the world was created. Creation was to make it appear as though there were two: Creator and creation. But Israel would receive the Torah beginning with the alef of “I am,” and so forth, to recognize that even now, after the world was created, Hashem is one, just as before its creation. This comes from the Torah, which sustains the world; from the world’s side there is bet. The beginning of the recognition of this twofoldness is in the heart, where there are two chambers dwelling places for the two inclinations. The evil inclination makes it appear that there are two, separating creation from the Creator, Heaven forbid; the good inclination guides him to know that in truth Hashem is one and there is nothing besides Him.
records.explanation: Pri Tzadik reconciles one originally good power of longing with two chambers of the heart, corresponding to Torah and worldly life. Likkutei Maamarim explains the spiritual danger behind the division: worldly life can be perceived as detached from its divine source. The connection supplies a conceptual account of the split without equating bodily activity itself with evil.

records.themeTitle: When ordinary delight serves a larger joy
records.themeSummary: Holy intention changes the place of physical enjoyment within a person’s life.
records.originHebrew: שֶׁבְּכָל עִנְיְנֵי הָעוֹלָם כְּשֶׁמְּכַוֵּין לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, הוּא עֲבוֹדָה לַמָּקוֹם וְהוּא מַעֲשֵׂה מִצְוָה. וּכְשֶׁמְּכַוֵּין לְשֵׁם תַּאֲוָה הוּא לְהֵיפֶךְ, וְאֵין דְּבַר רְשׁוּת כְּלָל.
records.originEnglish: In all worldly affairs, when one intends them for Heaven’s sake, it is service of God and an act of mitzvah. When one intends them for craving, it is the reverse; there is no merely neutral act at all.
records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Bereshit 1
records.targetHebrew: וְזֶהוּ פֵּירוּשׁ הַפָּסוּק (מִשְׁלֵי כג, כו) "תְּנָה בְנִי לִבְּךָ לִי", וּמִמֵּילָא "דְּרָכַי תִּצֹּרְנָה", הַיְינוּ כְּשֶׁתִּמְסוֹר לִבְּךָ לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אָז תִּהְיֶה אֶצְלְךָ עֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עִיקָּר וְכָל דִּבְרֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה טְפֵלִים לָזֶה, עַל דֶּרֶךְ מָשָׁל עָשִׁיר שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ בֵּן הָגוּן וְחָכָם וּמַשִּׂיא אוֹתוֹ אִשָּׁה לְפִי כְּבוֹדוֹ וּבְשָׁעָה שֶׁהֵכִין צָרְכֵי הַנִּשּׂוּאִין וְיִטְעַם מֵהַמַּאֲכָלִים שֶׁהֵכִין, בְּעֵת טָעֳמוֹ מֵהַמַּאֲכָל יִזְכּוֹר שִׂמְחַת בְּנוֹ וְהַטְּעִימָה אֶצְלוֹ טְפֵילָה וְהָבֵן.
records.targetEnglish: This is the meaning of the verse in Proverbs 23:26, “My son, give your heart to Me,” and consequently, “will keep My ways”: when you give your heart to Hashem, blessed be He, the service of Hashem becomes primary for you, and all matters of this world become secondary to it. By way of example, a wealthy man has a worthy and wise son and arranges a marriage for him befitting his honor. When he has prepared the wedding necessities and tastes the food he has prepared, as he tastes it he remembers his joy in his son; the tasting is secondary for him. Understand this.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach’s wedding analogy makes Pri Tzadik’s account of holy worldly activity concrete. The father still tastes the food, but its significance comes from his greater joy in his son. This explains a reordering of delight within divine service, rather than requiring that every physical sensation disappear.

records.themeTitle: How the promise of redemption is recognized
records.themeSummary: The sign of the redeemer is an awakened heart, including the divine help that awakens it.
records.originHebrew: הוּא כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ לְעִנְיַן קוּשְׁיַת רַבֵּנוּ מֹשֶׁה בֶּן נַחְמָן: מַה סִימָן מָסַר יוֹסֵף, שֶׁגּוֹאֵל שֶׁיֹּאמַר פְּקִידָה כְּפוּלָה גּוֹאֵל אֱמֶת הוּא? וְהָא אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁגַּם מֹשֶׁה שָׁמַע הַמָּסוֹרֶת כְּמוֹתָם. וְאָמַרְנוּ שֶׁהַסִּימָן הָיָה מִי שֶׁיַּכְנִיס אוֹר זֶה שֶׁל הַפְּקִידָה בְּלִבָּם, שֶׁיַּרְגִּישׁוּ בְּלִבָּם אוֹר מִפְּקִידָה, זֶהוּ הַגּוֹאֵל אֲמִיתִּי (וְנִתְבָּאֵר פָּרָשַׁת שְׁמוֹת מַאֲמָר ו, עַיֵּן שָׁם).
records.originEnglish: This follows what we explained concerning Ramban’s question: what sign did Joseph transmit, that a redeemer who speaks of remembrance twice is a true redeemer? Moses might also have heard the tradition as they had. We explained that the sign was the person who would bring this light of remembrance into their hearts, so that in their hearts they would feel the light of being remembered: he is the true redeemer. This was explained in Shemot, teaching 6; see there.
records.targetHebrew: אבל באמת מה שהקב"ה יפקוד ויזכור את ישראל הוא גם כן כמו שאתה הווה עמי וכמה שנאמר כמים הפנים לפנים וגו' דאמרו זה גם על הקב"ה (וכמ"ש ספרי דברים ע"פ בשנאת ה' אותנו וכו' מה דבליבך על רחמך וכו' ע"ש) וכשיעלה בזכרונינו אלהותו יתברך אז יזכור גם הוא אותנו. והגואל השליח דאנכי שלחתיך הוא יאיר להם האור הזה בלבם גם בגודל שיקועם וחשכות מצרים וזה סימן הגואל האמיתי שיוכל להכניס זה בלבם. והנה דצריך שאתה הווה עמי שההתחלה יהיה מאתערותא דלתתא אבל כשהגיע העת אז הוא המעוררם גם לאתערותא. וזה שא' על שאלת מה שמו היינו איזה תפיסה יוכל להיות בהם בגודל השיקוע בלא אתערותא מהם ועל זה א' אשר אהיה דגם מה שאתה הווה עמי אני אהיה גם ע"ז לעשות שתהיה אתה הווה עמי.
records.targetEnglish: But in truth, the Holy One’s taking notice of and remembering Israel also follows “As you are with Me,” as it says, “As water reflects face to face,” and so forth. They said this also concerning the Holy One, blessed be He, as in the Sifrei to Deuteronomy on “Because Hashem hates us”: what is in your heart toward your friend, and so forth; see there. When His divinity arises in our remembrance, He too will remember us. The redeemer, the messenger of “I have sent you,” will shine this light into their hearts even in their deep immersion and Egypt’s darkness. This is the sign of the true redeemer: that he can bring this into their hearts. Although “As you are with Me” requires the beginning to be an awakening from below, when the time arrives He also awakens them to that awakening. Moses asked, “What is His name?”—what grasp could they have in their great immersion, without an awakening on their part? To this He said, “That I will be”: even as regards your being with Me, I will be there too, to make you be with Me.
records.explanation: This is the earlier teaching Pri Tzadik explicitly directs the reader to. Its added step is that divine help initiates even the apparently human awakening needed for redemption. The doubled wording therefore expresses an inward event and its divine source, rather than a password that an impostor could repeat.

records.themeTitle: Receiving the act of eating as well as the food
records.themeSummary: Divine provision includes the way nourishment becomes holy.
records.originHebrew: וּכְתִיב בְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: וְנָתַן לִי לֶחֶם לֶאֱכוֹל וּבֶגֶד לִלְבּוֹשׁ. וְלָמָּה כְּתִיב לֶאֱכוֹל וְלִלְבּוֹשׁ? וּמִי לֹא יָדַע שֶׁהַלֶּחֶם לַאֲכִילָה וּבֶגֶד הוּא לִלְבּוֹשׁ? וּבְגֵר דִּכְתִיב לָתֶת לוֹ לֶחֶם וְשִׂמְלָה, לֹא כְּתִיב לֶחֶם לֶאֱכוֹל וְשִׂמְלָה לִלְבּוֹשׁ. רַק דְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בִּיקֵּשׁ שֶׁיִּתֵּן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לוֹ הַלֶּחֶם וְגַם הָאֲכִילָה, שֶׁיַּאֲכִילֵהוּ וְיִהְיֶה הָאֲכִילָה בִּקְדוּשָּׁה. וְכֵן שֶׁיִּתֵּן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַבֶּגֶד וְהַלְּבִישָׁה, שֶׁיַּלְבִּישֵׁהוּ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בִּלְבִישָׁה: וַיַּעַשׂ הַשֵּׁם אֱלֹהִים לְאָדָם וּלְאִשְׁתּוֹ כָּתְנוֹת עוֹר וַיַּלְבִּישֵׁם. דִּלְבַד שֶׁעָשָׂה לָהֶם הַכָּתְנוֹת, הִלְבִּישָׁם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
records.originEnglish: Of Jacob our father, peace be upon him, it is written: “He will give me bread to eat and clothing to wear.” Why does it say “to eat” and “to wear”? Who does not know that bread is for eating and clothing for wearing? Concerning the convert, where it says “to give him bread and clothing,” it does not say bread to eat and clothing to wear. Rather, Jacob asked that Hashem, blessed be He, give him the bread and also the eating—that He feed him, and that the eating be holy. Likewise, that Hashem give him the clothing and the dressing, that Hashem clothe him. As we find concerning dressing: “Hashem God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and clothed them.” Besides making the garments for them, Hashem clothed them.
records.targetHebrew: אמנם באמת הכל אחד הוא שהרועה ג"כ מנהיג צאנו בדרך הישר וגם מפרנסם וכמ"ש בזוה"ק (ח"ב כ ב) ופי' ה' רועי הוא ג"כ מפרנסני. והוא היסוד בהקדושה שעיקר שורש הסתת הנחש הי' בהרגש הנאת הגוף באכילה ואין יצה"ר שולט אלא מתוך אכילה ושתיה כמש"נ ואכלת ושבעת השמרו לכם וגו' ובספרי מייתי לה מכמה פסוקים. וכשהש"י הרועה ומפרנס הוא בקדושה וכמו שביקש שהמע"ה הטריפני לחם חוקי שיהיה הש"י הזן לחם הנחקק ונקצב כמה שנצרך לתורה ועבודה. וחוקי מורה שנחקק בלב הד"ת והעבודה ע"י האכילה וממילא בא ההנהגה בדרך הישר על מי מנוחות ינהלני נפשי ישובב שנדרש (שוח"ט תהלים) על ד"ת. ינחני במעגלי צדק וגו'
records.targetEnglish: In truth it is all one: the shepherd both guides his flock on the right path and provides for them, as stated in the holy Zohar, volume II, 20b. The meaning of “Hashem is my shepherd” is also “He provides for me.” This is the foundation of holiness, for the root of the serpent’s enticement was the sensation of bodily pleasure in eating, and the evil inclination rules only through eating and drinking, as it says, “You shall eat and be satisfied; take care,” and so forth; the Sifrei brings several verses for this. When Hashem is the shepherd and provider, it is holy. As King Solomon, peace be upon him, asked, “Provide me with my allotted bread”: that Hashem be the One who nourishes him with the bread determined and allotted according to what is needed for Torah and service. “My allotment” also indicates that words of Torah and service become engraved in the heart through eating. Guidance on the right path follows of itself: “He leads me beside restful waters; He restores my soul,” interpreted in the Midrash on Psalms as words of Torah; “He guides me in paths of righteousness,” and so forth.
records.explanation: Vayechi develops the shepherd image used in this Shevat teaching. The same divine provision nourishes the body and directs the soul; properly allotted food engraves Torah in the heart. This explains why Jacob requests the holy act of eating itself in addition to possession of bread.

records.themeTitle: Shabbat joins bodily delight with preparation
records.themeSummary: The holiness of enjoyment includes the limits that make it a Shabbat act.
records.originHebrew: וְכֵן אֲכִילַת שַׁבָּת שֶׁהִיא בִּקְדוּשָּׁה, אִיתָא מֵהָאֲרִי זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה, שֶׁכָּל מַה שֶּׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל אוֹכֵל בְּשַׁבָּת, אַף לַהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ, הוּא בִּקְדוּשָּׁה. וְזֶהוּ הִמְלִיךְ אוֹת צָדִי בִּלְעִיטָה, לְתַקֵּן הָאֲכִילָה, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַמַּאֲכִיל וְיִהְיֶה אֲכִילָה בִּקְדוּשָּׁה.
records.originEnglish: Likewise, Shabbat eating is holy. It is taught in the name of the Ari, of blessed memory, that everything a Jew eats on Shabbat, even for his own enjoyment, is holy. This is “He made the letter tzadi reign over swallowing”: to repair eating, so that Hashem, blessed be He, is the One who feeds him and the eating is holy.
records.targetRef: Sod Yesharim, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot 3:3
records.targetHebrew: אמנם בשבת נכללו שניהם ביחד התפשטות וגם צמצום כי בשבת גם הנאת הגוף הוא מצוה ומקיים בזאת ההנאה מצות עשה וקראת לשבת עונג הרי שיש בו גודל התפשטות גם מצד האדם ויש בו נמי מצד האדם גודל צמצום כי אין מותר בשבת רק מן המוכן ומי שטרח בערב שבת יאכל בשבת ואם לא טרח מערב שבת אין לו בשבת מה לאכול הרי שיש בו נמי גודל צמצום:
records.targetEnglish: On Shabbat, however, both are included together: expansion and also restraint. For on Shabbat bodily enjoyment too is a mitzvah, and through this enjoyment one fulfills the positive command, “You shall call Shabbat a delight.” Thus it contains great expansion even from the person’s side. It also contains great restraint from the person’s side, for on Shabbat only what has been prepared is permitted. One who labored on the eve of Shabbat will eat on Shabbat, while one who did not labor beforehand has nothing to eat on Shabbat. Thus it also contains great restraint.
records.explanation: The surrounding Sod Yesharim paragraphs distinguish God’s broad provision from the person’s need to avoid unmeasured enjoyment. The selected conclusion joins the two in Shabbat: bodily delight is commanded, and prior preparation bounds it. It therefore sharpens the Shevat passage without turning its praise of holy enjoyment into unrestricted consumption.

records.themeTitle: Allotted bread and the limits of abstinence
records.themeSummary: Refining appetite aims at holy nourishment and includes a limit on excessive fasting.
records.originHebrew: וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר טֶרֶף נָתַן לִירֵאָיו, וְכֵן וַתִּתֵּן טֶרֶף לְבֵיתָהּ וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁהַיְּרֵאִים אוֹכְלִים רַק כְּטֶרֶף הַזְּאֵב, שֶׁלֹּא לַהֲנָאַת הַגּוּף. וַאֲכִילָתָם הוּא לְקִיּוּם הַחַיִּים לְבַדּוֹ, שֶׁכֵּן בָּרָא הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הָאָדָם נִצְרָךְ לְהַכְנִיס בְּתוֹכוֹ מַאֲכָל לְקִיּוּם הַחַיִּים, וְנַעֲשָׂה רְצוֹנוֹ בָּזֶה. וְזֶהוּ וַתִּתֵּן טֶרֶף לְבֵיתָהּ, הֵם הַתַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁהֵם בְּנֵי בֵיתָהּ שֶׁל הַכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל כַּיָּדוּעַ. וְחוֹק לְנַעֲרוֹתֶיהָ, וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר הַטְרִיפֵנִי לֶחֶם חוּקִּי, שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּעַצְמוֹ יִהְיֶה הַמַּאֲכִיל וְהַמַּטְרִיף. וְזֶה כְּמוֹ לְעִיטָה, שֶׁהָאָדָם פּוֹתֵחַ פִּיו וּמַלְעִיטִין אוֹתוֹ וְאֵינוֹ מַרְגִּישׁ טַעַם הַמַּאֲכָל בְּחִכּוֹ. וְזֶהוּ לֶחֶם חוּקִּי שֶׁחוֹקֵק עַל יְדֵי זֶה הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה בַּלֵּב. שֶׁהַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה נִקְרָא לֶחֶם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: לְכוּ לַחֲמוּ בְלַחֲמִי, וּבַזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ג רעא ב): נַהֲמָא דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא דְּבִכְתָב. וְזֶה שֶׁכָּתוּב הִמְלִיךְ אוֹת צ׳ בִּלְעִיטָה וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁעֵסֶק הַחוֹדֶשׁ לְתַקֵּן הָאֲכִילָה, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה צַדִּיק אוֹכֵל רַק לְשׂוֹבַע נַפְשׁוֹ, שֶׁיִּשְׂבַּע הַנֶּפֶשׁ שְׂבִיעָה בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה, כַּאֲכִילַת שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם (שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים).
records.originEnglish: This is “He gave prey to those who fear Him,” and likewise, “She gives provision to her household,” and so forth: those who fear Him eat only as a wolf seizes prey, without seeking bodily enjoyment. Their eating is solely to sustain life, for Hashem created the person to need to take food into himself to sustain life, and His will is thereby fulfilled. “She gives provision to her household” refers to Torah scholars, who are members of the household of the Congregation of Israel, as is known. “And an allotment to her maidens”: this is “Provide me with my allotted bread,” that Hashem Himself be the One who feeds and provides. It resembles being fed: a person opens his mouth and is fed, without feeling the food’s taste on his palate. This is “my allotted bread,” through which words of Torah become engraved in the heart. Words of Torah are called bread, as it says, “Come, eat of My bread,” and the holy Zohar, volume III, 271b, speaks of “the bread of the Written Torah.” This is “He made the letter tzadi reign over swallowing,” and so forth: the month’s work is to repair eating, so that the righteous person eats only to satisfy his soul, that the soul be satisfied with words of Torah, like King Solomon’s eating, as explained several times.
records.targetHebrew: וּבִקֵּשׁ עַל הַמַּאֲכָל שֶׁיִּהְיֶה גַּם כֵּן "טֶרֶף", וְזֶהוּ עַל יְדֵי "לֶחֶם חֻקִּי", בְּהַגְדָּרָה, לֹא בְּרַעַבְתָנוּת וְשֶׁפַע תַּאֲוָה הַנִּקְרָא "עֹשֶׁר", וְלֹא בְּהַכְפָּנָה יְתֵרָה וְרֵישׁוּת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: הַיּוֹשֵׁב בְּתַעֲנִית נִקְרָא חוֹטֵא פֵּרוּשׁ, שֶׁמְּחַסֵּר הַעֲלָאַת הַקְּדֻשָּׁה שֶׁבַּמַּאֲכָל לִמְקוֹמָהּ עַל יְדֵי הָאֲכִילָה; וְרַק "בֶּטֶן רְשָׁעִים תֶּחְסָר", רָאוּי לֶאֱסֹר וּלְהִתְעַנּוֹת כְּדֵי לְכַלּוֹת הָרַעַבְתָנוּת; אֲבָל צַדִּיק שֶׁאֵינוֹ רַעַבְתָן וְשָׁטוּף בְּתַאֲוָה, "אוֹכֵל לְשֹׂבַע נַפְשׁוֹ", הַיְינוּ לֶחֶם חֻקִּי, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יוּכַל לְהַגִּיעַ לְדַרְגַּת "הַטְרִיפֵנִי", שֶׁיִּהְיֶה טוֹרֵף וְחוֹטֵף הַטּוֹב שֶׁבָּרָע לְכַלֵּל בַּטּוֹב. וְזֶה טַעַם "טֶרֶף נָתַן לִירֵאָיו": הַיְּרֵאִים הֵם הַמֻּגְדָּרִים בְּתַאֲווֹת בְּיוֹתֵר, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה בָּא לִכְלַל מְנִיעַת אֲכִילַת לֶחֶם חֻקִּי גַּם כֵּן, וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא נוֹתֵן לָהֶם בְּמַתָּנָה "טֶרֶף", לֶאֱכֹל לֶחֶם חֻקִּי עַל כָּל פָּנִים, כְּדֵי לִטְרֹף אוֹתָם הַנִּיצוֹצוֹת קְדוֹשִׁים שֶׁבַּמַּאֲכָל.
records.targetEnglish: He asked that food too should be “prey.” This comes through “my allotted bread,” within a limit: neither ravenousness and an abundance of craving, called wealth, nor excessive starvation and poverty. As it is taught, one who sits fasting is called a sinner—meaning that he diminishes the elevation of the holiness in food to its place through eating. Only “the belly of the wicked shall lack”: for him restriction and fasting are fitting, to consume his ravenousness. But a righteous person who is not ravenous and immersed in craving “eats to satisfy his soul”—that is, his allotted bread. Through this he can reach the level of “provide me with prey,” seizing the good within evil to include it in the good. This is the meaning of “He gave prey to those who fear Him”: those who fear Him restrict their desires excessively and thereby come to refrain even from eating their allotted bread. The Holy One, blessed be He, gives them “prey” as a gift—to eat their allotted bread at least, so as to seize those holy sparks within the food.
records.explanation: Et HaOchel develops the same linked expressions, “prey” and “allotted bread,” but explicitly supplies the balancing condition: a person can also obstruct the task by excessive abstinence. This keeps the Shevat passage’s account of ascetic practices in its larger spiritual context.

records.themeSummary: Enduring joy requires the removal of what separates the heart from divine service.
records.originHebrew: וְאָמְרוּ (תַּעֲנִית טו.): צַדִּיקִים לְאוֹרָה וִישָׁרִים לְשִׂמְחָה, לְיִשְׁרֵי לֵב שִׂמְחָה. שֶׁהַשִּׂמְחָה רַק כְּשֶׁמִּתְבַּטֵּל הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע מִכֹּל וָכֹל, וּמִתְיַישֵּׁר הַלֵּב לִהְיוֹת לֵב אֶחָד לְאָבִיו שֶׁבַּשָּׁמַיִם, וְאָז אֵין לוֹ שׁוּם מִלְחָמָה עִם הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע וְזוֹכֶה לְשִׂמְחָה (וְנִתְבָּאֵר כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים). וּבֶאֱמֶת מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יִזְכּוּ עַל יְדֵי מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן יוֹסֵף לְיַשְׁרוּת הַלֵּב, דִּכְתִיב: אוֹר צַדִּיקִים יִשְׂמָח. וְהַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי הָאוֹר זָרוּעַ לַצַּדִּיק, שֶׁזּוֹכֶה עַל יְדֵי בְּחִינַת צַדִּיק כְּשֶׁמִּתְגַּבֵּר עַל יִצְרוֹ. זוֹכֶה אַחַר כָּךְ לְייַשֵּׁר הַלֵּב מִכֹּל וָכֹל, וְזוֹכֶה לְשִׂמְחָה הַמְּיוּחָד לְיִשְׁרֵי לֵב.
records.originEnglish: They said in Ta’anit 15a: light is for the righteous and joy for the upright—“joy for the upright of heart.” Joy comes only when the evil inclination is entirely nullified and the heart becomes upright, one heart devoted to its Father in heaven. Then there is no further battle with the evil inclination, and one merits joy, as explained several times. In truth, from Hashem’s side they will merit uprightness of heart through Mashiach ben Yosef, for it is written, “The light of the righteous rejoices.” Through “light sown for the righteous,” which one merits through the quality of righteousness when overcoming the inclination, one subsequently merits making the heart entirely upright and attaining the joy particular to the upright of heart.
records.targetHebrew: וּבָזֶה זוֹכֶה לְשִׂמְחַת לֵב מְבַקְשֵׁי ה', דְּ"שִׂמְחוּ צַדִּיקִים בַּה'" כְּתִיב, שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַשִּׂמְחָה שֶׁרוֹצֶה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּעוֹלָמוֹ, דְּ"יִשְׂמַח יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּעֹשָׂיו", וְזֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר אֶלָּא כְּשֶׁנִּסְתַּלֵּק הַמָּסָךְ הַחוֹצֵץ, דְּעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְּבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ (רַבָּה פֶּרֶק ג׳): "אֲנִי יָרֵאתִי מִתּוֹךְ שִׂמְחָתִי וְשָׂמַחְתִּי מִתּוֹךְ יִרְאָתִי", דְּשִׂמְחַת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא רַק הַבָּאָה מִתּוֹךְ הַיִּרְאָה, דְּעַל כֵּן נֶאֱמַר: "עִבְדוּ אֶת ה' בְּיִרְאָה" וְ"עִבְדוּ אֶת ה' בְּשִׂמְחָה", דְּצָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת שְׁנֵיהֶם יַחַד (עַיֵּן בְּרָכוֹת ל׳ עַמּוּד ב׳); וְזֶהוּ שִׂמְחָה הָרְאוּיָה, לְאַפּוֹקֵי שִׂמְחָה שֶׁל הוֹלֵלוּת עַל יְדֵי מִלּוּי תַּאֲווֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְכַיּוֹצֵא לְמִי שֶׁלֹּא זָכָה דְּנַעֲשֵׂית לוֹ סַם הַמָּוֶת (יוֹמָא ע״ב עַמּוּד ב׳), כִּי טַעַם מֵהַיַּיִן שֶׁהֵבִיא יְלָלָה לָעוֹלָם, דְּמִי שֶׁלֹּא זָכָה — מְשַׁמַּמְתּוֹ (שָׁם ע״ו עַמּוּד ב׳), שֶׁשִּׂמְחָה זוֹ לְפִי שָׁעָה, וְסוֹף נַעֲשֶׂה שׁוֹמֵם וְרֵיקָן מִכֹּל עַל יְדֵי זֶה; וְזֶהוּ פְּסֹלֶת הַגְּבוּרָה שֶׁקָּלַט עֵשָׂו, דְּ"עַל חַרְבְּךָ תִחְיֶה", שֶׁנָּטַל הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְחֶלְקוֹ לִשְׂמֹחַ בְּשִׂמְחַת שָׁעָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, דְּעַל זֶה אָמַר: "הִנֵּה מִשְׁמַנֵּי [הָאָרֶץ יִהְיֶה מוֹשָׁבֶךָ]" וְגוֹמֵר, דְּאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה שֶׁבִּרְכָתוֹ הוּא דָּבָר הַמְזֻמָּן, כִּי לְשִׂמְחָה דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵין צָרִיךְ הֲכָנָה, כִּי הוּא מוּכָן וְעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי כָּל הָרוֹצֶה לֵילֵךְ בִּשְׁרִירוּת לִבּוֹ וְלִפְרֹק עֹל, מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הַשִּׂמְחָה שֶׁל אֱמֶת לֹא בְּקַל לִזְכּוֹת לָהּ.
records.targetEnglish: Through this one merits the heart’s joy of those who seek Hashem, for it is written, “Rejoice in Hashem, you righteous.” This is the joy Hashem desires in His world: “Let Israel rejoice in its Maker.” It is possible only when the intervening screen is removed. Thus Tanna Devei Eliyahu, Rabbah chapter 3, says: “I feared through my joy, and rejoiced through my fear.” Israel’s joy is only that which comes through awe. It therefore says both “Serve Hashem with awe” and “Serve Hashem with joy,” for the two must be together; see Berakhot 30b. This is fitting joy, excluding the joy of frivolity through satisfying worldly cravings, and the like, for one who has not merited it and for whom it becomes a potion of death, as in Yoma 72b. He has tasted the wine that brought wailing to the world: one who does not merit it is laid waste by it, as stated there, 76b. That joy is momentary, and through it he finally becomes desolate and empty of everything. This is the dross of might that Esau absorbed—“By your sword you shall live.” He took this world as his portion, to rejoice in its momentary joy. Of this it says, “Your dwelling shall be of the richness of the earth,” and so forth; the sages said that his blessing concerns what is already available. Joy in this world requires no preparation: it is ready for anyone who wishes to follow his heart’s stubbornness and throw off the yoke. True joy, however, is not easily attained.
records.explanation: The origin distinguishes an actual repair of the heart from the later recognition of that repair in the messianic sequence. Divrei Soferim explains the quality of joy itself: it comes with awe and removal of an inner screen, unlike transient gratification. It adds a criterion for understanding “joy of the heart” without importing its separate Esau narrative into Pri Tzadik’s chronology.

records.themeSummary: Joining mind and heart gives religious speech its inward content.
records.originHebrew: וְזֶה שֶׁכָּתוּב: זֶה צַדִּיקוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם שֶׁהוּא עוֹשֶׂה צְדָקוֹת כוּלֵי, זוֹ דַּעַת חָכְמָה וּבִינָה, שֶׁהַדַּעַת בְּחִבּוּר חָכְמָה שֶׁבַּמּוֹחַ עִם בִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ עַל מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: כִּי תָבוֹא חָכְמָה בְלִבֶּךָ וְדַעַת וְגוֹמֵר (וְנִתְבָּאֵר כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים). וְהַיְינוּ ג׳ רִאשׁוֹנוֹת, י״ה עִם קוּצָא דְיוּד דִּלְעֵילָא שֶׁרוֹמֵז לְכֶתֶר עֶלְיוֹן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (שָׁם סה ב), וְדַעַת פְּנִימִיּוּת הַכֶּתֶר כַּיָּדוּעַ. וּפְתִיחַת פֶּה וּמַעֲנֵה לָשׁוֹן שֶׁהוּא נוֹתֵן לִבְנֵי אָדָם, הַיְינוּ מַלְכוּת פֶּה, תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה קָרִינַן לָהּ.
records.originEnglish: This is what it says: “This is the Righteous One of the world, who performs acts of righteousness,” and so forth—“this is knowledge, wisdom, and understanding.” Knowledge lies in joining the wisdom in the mind with the understanding in the heart, as we explained concerning “For wisdom will enter your heart, and knowledge,” and so forth, explained several times. These are the first three, yud-heh with the upper tip of the yud alluding to supernal Keter, as stated in the holy Zohar there, 65b; knowledge is the inward aspect of Keter, as is known. “And the opening of the mouth and the tongue’s response, which He gives human beings”: this is “Malchut is the mouth; we call it the Oral Torah.”
records.targetHebrew: וְהַמַּעֲלָה הַשְּׁלִישִׁית הַבָּאָה עַל יְדֵי הָעֲבוֹדָה הִיא קִשּׁוּר הַמֹּחַ עִם הַלֵּב בְּיַחַד. וְהוּא מַעֲלַת הַנְּבוּאָה, שֶׁיָּדוּעַ שֶׁשֹּׁרֶשׁ מִלַּת "נָבִיא" מִן "נִיב שְׂפָתָיִם" [יְשַׁעְיָהוּ נ״ז:י״ט], שֶׁרָצָה לוֹמַר דַּבְּרָן, וְהַיְינוּ שְׁלֵמוּת כֹּחַ הַדִּבּוּר הַמִּתְיַחֵס אֶל הַלֵּב כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר לְעֵיל. וְלָכֵן לַנָּבִיא יִקְרְאוּ לְפָנִים בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל "הָרֹאֶה" (שְׁמוּאֵל א ט׳:ט׳), כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (בְּקֹהֶלֶת א׳:ט״ז): "וְלִבִּי רָאָה הַרְבֵּה חָכְמָה", שֶׁהָרְאִיָּה גַּם הִיא מִתְיַחֶסֶת אֶל הַלֵּב כַּאֲשֶׁר הִיא מִתְקַשֶּׁרֶת וּמִתְאַחֶדֶת עִם הַחָכְמָה שֶׁבַּמֹּחַ. וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁהַרְגָּשַׁת הַלֵּב בְּאַחְדוּת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא מִצַּד הַחָכְמָה וְהַיְּדִיעָה, וְהֵם מְיֻחָדִים כְּעִנְיַן (פֶּרֶק ג׳ [ב׳] דְּאָבוֹת [מִשְׁנָה ט׳/י״ז]): "אִם אֵין יִרְאָה אֵין חָכְמָה, אִם אֵין חָכְמָה אֵין יִרְאָה".
records.targetEnglish: The third excellence that comes through service is the joining of mind and heart together. This is the excellence of prophecy, for, as is known, the root of the word “prophet” is “utterance of the lips,” in Isaiah 57:19, meaning a speaker: the perfection of the power of speech, which belongs to the heart, as explained above. Therefore a prophet was formerly called “the seer” in Israel, as in I Samuel 9:9, and as it says in Ecclesiastes 1:16, “My heart has seen much wisdom.” Seeing too belongs to the heart when it is joined and united with the wisdom of the mind. That is, the heart’s feeling of Hashem’s unity comes from wisdom and knowledge, and they are united, in the manner of the saying in Avot: “If there is no awe, there is no wisdom; if there is no wisdom, there is no awe.”
records.explanation: Pri Tzadik presents mind, heart, and speech as divine gifts joined through the tzadi. Sichat Malakhei HaSharet supplies the inner account of that joining: the heart’s felt recognition grows from knowledge and takes form in speech. Its full paragraph goes on to distinguish Moses’ and Isaiah’s prophetic qualities, so the connection concerns the mechanism of joining rather than asserting that all forms of inspired speech are identical.

records.themeTitle: From God’s Torah to Torah that becomes one’s own
records.themeSummary: Moses’ later speech is read as the fruit of an earlier inward acquisition.
records.originHebrew: וְאָמַר עוֹד: וּבִשְׁבִיל שֶׁאָמַר מֹשֶׁה כִּי כְבַד פֶּה וְלֹא אִישׁ דְּבָרִים אָנֹכִי, זָכָה שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: פֶּה אֶל פֶּה אֲדַבֶּר בּוֹ, וְזָכָה שֶׁאָמַר אֵלֶּה הַדְּבָרִים. וְהוּא כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה דְּבָרִים ב וּמִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה שָׁם): אֶתְמוֹל אָמַרְתָּ לֹא אִישׁ דְּבָרִים אָנֹכִי, וְעַכְשָׁיו אַתָּה מְדַבֵּר כָּל כָּךְ וְכוּלֵי; שָׁנָה אֶת הַתּוֹרָה וְהִתְרַפֵּא כוּלֵי. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: מַרְפֵּא לָשׁוֹן עֵץ חַיִּים. וְסֵפֶר דְּבָרִים הוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ כָּל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זוֹהַר חֵלֶק ג רסא א: תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב וְתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, וְהוּא אִקְרֵי תּוֹרָה וּמִשְׁנֵה תוֹרָה. וְזֶה אָמַר מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּרֹאשׁ חוֹדֶשׁ שְׁבָט, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: בְּעַשְׁתֵּי עָשָׂר חוֹדֶשׁ בְּא׳ לַחוֹדֶשׁ דִּיבֶּר מֹשֶׁה וְגוֹמֵר, חוֹדֶשׁ שֶׁנּוֹצַר בְּאוֹת צ׳.
records.originEnglish: It further says: because Moses said, “I am heavy of mouth,” and “I am not a man of words,” he merited the Holy One’s saying to him, “Mouth to mouth I speak with him,” and merited saying, “These are the words.” This is as stated in Tanchuma, Devarim 2, and in the Midrash Rabbah there: “Yesterday you said, ‘I am not a man of words,’ and now you speak so much,” and so forth; “Study the Torah and be healed,” and so forth. As it says, “A healing tongue is a tree of life.” The book of Deuteronomy is the root of the whole Oral Torah, as stated in Zohar III, 261a: “The Written Torah and the Oral Torah,” and “it is called Torah and Mishneh Torah.” Moses our teacher said this on Rosh Chodesh Shevat, as it says, “In the eleventh month, on the first of the month, Moses spoke,” and so forth—the month formed with the letter tzadi.
records.targetHebrew: וּמִמַּה שֶּׁכָּתוּב שָׁם: אַגְמִירוּ וְכוּלֵי כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלִיגְרְסוּ, נִרְאֶה דִּבְהַתְחָלָה צָרִיךְ לְיַגֵּעַ שֶׁיִּהְיוּ דְּבָרִים הַיּוֹצְאִים מִן הַלֵּב; אֲבָל אַחַר כָּךְ זוֹכֶה לְדִבּוּר וְגִירְסָא הֲגַם דְּלָא יָדַע מַאי קָאָמַר, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא פִּטְטַיָּא דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא, גַּם כֵּן הוּא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה גָּמוּר. וְהוּא מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (שָׁם): בַּתְּחִלָּה תּוֹרַת ה', וְאַחַר כָּךְ תּוֹרָתוֹ; וּכְשֶׁזּוֹכֶה דְּהוּא תּוֹרָתוֹ, דּוּגְמַת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נַעֲשׂוּ שְׁתֵּי כִּלְיוֹתָיו וְכוּלֵי (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סא), גַּם דִּבּוּר שֶׁהוּא מֵהַשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ הוּא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה. וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בְּדוֹאֵג בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (קו:) שֶׁכָּל תּוֹרָתוֹ וְכוּלֵי מִשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ, הַיְינוּ בְּלֹא הָיָה לוֹ הַהַתְחָלָה; וְגַם כִּי עַל יְדֵי לָשׁוֹן הָרָע נִתְקַלְקֵל הַדִּבּוּר שֶׁמֵּהַשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ.
records.targetEnglish: From what is said there, “Teach them,” and so forth, “so that they may recite,” it appears that at the beginning one must labor so that the words come from the heart. But afterward one merits speech and recitation, even when one does not know what one is saying: this is called the chatter of Torah, and it too is fully words of Torah. This is what is said in Avodah Zarah there: first it is Hashem’s Torah, and afterward it is his Torah. When one merits its becoming his Torah, like Abraham our father, peace be upon him, whose two kidneys became—and so forth, as in Bereshit Rabbah chapter 61—even speech from the lips outward is words of Torah. What is said of Doeg in Sanhedrin 106b, that all his Torah was—and so forth—“from the lips outward,” refers to his lacking that beginning. Also, through slander, speech from the lips outward became corrupted.
records.explanation: The full Tzidkat passage itself proceeds to “These are the words” and Moses speaking Deuteronomy from his own mouth. Its added condition is crucial: spontaneous or outward speech becomes Torah only after an inward, laborious beginning; Doeg is the counterexample. This explains the origin’s transformation of Moses’ speech without making every unconsidered utterance inspired.

records.themeSummary: A difficulty in speech can be read in relation to the task of bringing a higher light into shared life.
records.originHebrew: אֲנִי נוֹתֵן לְךָ פִּתְחוֹן פֶּה וּמַעֲנֵה לָשׁוֹן יוֹתֵר מִכָּל בָּאֵי עוֹלָם וְכוּלֵי. וְהַיְינוּ מִדַּת מַלְכוּת פֶּה, וְשַׁבָּת דִּבּוּר אִקְרֵי, וְהֵם שְׁנֵיהֶם תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה: פִּתְחוֹן פֶּה וּמַעֲנֵה לָשׁוֹן. וּמַסִּיק: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וְאָנֹכִי אֶהְיֶה עִם פִּיךָ וְהוֹרֵיתִיךָ וְכוּלֵי; עִם פִּיךָ, זוֹ פְּתִיחַת פֶּה וּמַעֲנֵה לָשׁוֹן, וְזֶה שֶׁכָּתוּב וְהוֹרֵיתִיךָ, זֶה גִּנְזֵי חָכְמָה שֶׁגִּלָּה לוֹ כוּלֵי.
records.originEnglish: I give you an opening of the mouth and a response of the tongue greater than those of all who come into the world, and so forth. This is the quality of Malchut, the mouth; Shabbat is called speech, and both are the Oral Torah: opening of the mouth and the tongue’s response. It concludes: “And I will be with your mouth and instruct you,” and so forth. “With your mouth”—this is the opening of the mouth and the tongue’s response; “and I will instruct you”—these are the treasures of wisdom that He revealed to him, and so forth.
records.targetHebrew: ומדרגה העליונה כזו נקרא בד"ת כבד פה וכבד לשון היינו שהגוף של מ"ר היה משולל גמר אף שמצד הנפש היו בו מיד כל השלימות עוד מיום הולדו אכן מה שנקרא שלימות מצד הגוף זאת לא היה יתכן שיגמר אצלו רק ביום מותו לכן משבח כ"כ הכתוב את יום מותו כי גמר השלימות מצד הגוף של מ"ר הוא כדכתיב הנך שוכב עם אבותיך וקם וכמבואר בזוה"ק (חקת קפב:) אע"ג דתתכנש הנך קיים לאנהרא לסיהרא וכו' היינו שיתכלל אורו של מ"ר בששים רבוא נפשות ישראל וממילא כאשר קם לאנהרא לסיהרא להיות נכלל אפילו בהנפש הנמוך שבישראל אזי נגמר אצלו השלימות גם מצד הגוף ושלימות כזאת אי אפשר רק בעת הסתלקותו לזה משבח כ"כ הכתוב את יום מותו:
records.targetEnglish: Such a lofty level is called in words of Torah “heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue”: Moses our teacher’s body was lacking completion, although from the soul’s side every perfection was his from the day of his birth. But what is called completion from the body’s side could be finished for him only on the day of his death. Therefore Scripture so greatly praises the day of his death. For the completion of Moses’ perfection from the body’s side is as it is written, “You lie with your fathers—and arise,” and as explained in the holy Zohar, Chukkat 182b: “Though you are gathered in, you remain to illumine the moon,” and so forth. This means that Moses’ light becomes included in the six hundred thousand souls of Israel. Consequently, when he arises to illumine the moon, becoming included even in the lowest soul in Israel, his perfection is completed from the body’s side as well. Such perfection is possible only at his departure; Scripture therefore so greatly praises the day of his death.
records.explanation: Both teachings refuse to treat Moses’ “heavy mouth” as a simple absence of spiritual capacity. Sod Yesharim interprets it through a higher light not yet fully brought into embodied life, whose completion reaches every Israelite soul. This offers a distinct perspective on Torah’s becoming a shared gift; its completion at Moses’ death is not identified with the origin’s earlier Rosh Chodesh Shevat event.
